SM17A-A2.free_elimination: Parity: the stem says the maximum equals 5 more than TWICE an integer value, so c must be odd. That strikes 6 with no setup beyond 'the max of -2(x-3)^2+c is c'. Sign: no constraint (c may be negative). Monotonicity/asymptote: none. Simplified-stem: -21 and 59 are the sign-slip and wrong-vertex variants, not visible free. Closure: none. Printed-number echo: none (3, 1, 5 do not appear as options).
SM17A-A2.note: Key verified independently. Labelled hard; it is a two-line linear equation after one substitution, and back-substituting each option is a single check, so medium at best on the hard route. All three distractor paths are real misreadings and reproduce their values.

SM17A-A3.free_elimination: Printed-number echo: 48 sits within 3 of the printed 45 and is the only option of that magnitude - it is the 'a = 45 un-computed' shape and is strikeable as an echo. Sign: all positive, no help. Monotonicity: a+b with b>1 and a*b^2=45 gives no cheap bound separating 8/15/18. Closure: 15 is the product a*b and 8 the sum, but that pair is not identifiable without solving. Parity: none.
SM17A-A3.note: Standard ratio-eliminates-a item, correct throughout. The 'product instead of sum' distractor (15) is the strongest of the three; 48 is weak because it is visibly an echo of a printed value.

SM17A-A4.free_elimination: Printed-number product: the target form (3x+a)/(x-b) is the original (5x+12)/(x-3) with the 5 and 3 swapped, a pattern a solver can apply by recognition rather than algebra, and 60 is the only option equal to 5*12. 15 (=3*5) and 36 (=3*12) are also products of printed pairs, so the echo channel does not by itself pick the key; 17 is the sum-when-a-product-is-asked option. Sign, monotonicity, parity: nothing.
SM17A-A4.note: Labelled easy; inverting a Mobius function and then reporting a product is a medium on the real module 2. A student who has memorised the coefficient swap gets it without doing the algebra, which is the item's main weakness but is genuine content knowledge, not a leak.

SM17A-A5.free_elimination: Simplified stem: 40 is b alone, the answer with the 'a +' dropped, and it is the only option that is also the value of the numerator at x=0 - strikeable as a partial. Parity would strike 40 as well (a is odd, b even, so a+b is odd) but only after the two expansions, so by the stated rule it does not count as a free strike. Sign: all positive. Closure/echo: none; no printed constant (7, 4, 2, 3, 6, 12) appears as an option.
SM17A-A5.note: Denominator factors exactly as printed, numerator is 13x+40. The explanation's own remark that neither constant is readable by inspection is correct: both a and b require the same expansion.

SM17A-A6.free_elimination: none found. All four options are odd, so parity is matched. The set is {key, key+4, key-6, key+12}, i.e. each distractor is the key with exactly one of the four constants perturbed, which is a coherent design but leaves the key in no distinguished position. No printed coefficient (2, -3, 5, 7, -4) appears as an option except the 5 that happens to BE the key - worth noting as an accidental echo, but it does not point the wrong way.
SM17A-A6.note: Verified by multiplying the quotient back: (x^2+2)(2x^2-3x+1)+13x-6 reproduces the dividend. Genuinely hard: four constants, two division steps, no shortcut. Best item in the batch.

SM17A-A7.free_elimination: Printed-number echo: -14 is exactly -10 minus 4, a bare difference of two printed constants, and 10 is the printed 10 with its sign flipped. Both are strikeable by echo without forming the difference quadratic. -1 is the sum of the x-coordinates (the answer with the line substitution dropped) but is not identifiable as such for free. Sign: y1+y2 = 2(x1+x2)+8 gives no free sign bound. Parity: all four differ in parity mix, no help.
SM17A-A7.note: Key correct via Vieta on x^2+x-14. EDITORIAL DEFECT: the explanation contains reviewer-facing meta-text ('that is what makes -14 the one strikeable option ... it is recorded here so that a grader locates it correctly'). That must not ship in a student-facing field, and the author's self-declared count of one strike understates it - the sign-flipped 10 is a second echo.

SM17A-A8.free_elimination: none found, and the option set is unusually well matched: all four of -42, 18, 30, 66 are divisible by 6, so both the mod-3 and the parity channels are closed. Closure: 30 is key+12 where 12 is the printed constant term, which is a real structural relation but does not say which of the pair is the key. Monotonicity/sign: p(3) could be of either sign a priori.
SM17A-A8.note: Two conditions, a 2x2 system, then the remainder theorem: correctly hard. a=-6, b=10, p(3)=18 confirmed. The 66 path (both signs reversed, satisfying neither condition) is the least natural of the three slips but still reproduces its value.

SM17A-B1.free_elimination: Closure under the printed number: 6 and 25 multiply to exactly 150, the printed minimum magnitude, so they form a manufactured divide-by-the-wrong-thing pair (150/6 and 150/25) and a solver who spots that strikes both without arithmetic, leaving 24 against 60 at 50/50. Sign: a must be positive for a minimum to exist, but all four options are positive so nothing falls. Monotonicity: none. Parity/echo: no printed constant appears as an option.
SM17A-B1.note: Key correct: half-gap is 2.5, depth is 6.25a = 150, a = 24. The reciprocal pair 6/25 is the weakness - two of three distractors are visibly generated from 150 by the same division and can be discarded together. Replacing one of them with a value not of the form 150/n would close it.

SM17A-B2.free_elimination: none found on the option set itself - the author closed both channels it declared and the declarations check out: v-16 is a perfect square for all four (9, 16, 25, 49) and all four exceed the right-hand side 21. But closing the perfect-square channel is exactly what makes back-substitution free: each option reduces to one subtraction and one exact square root (25->13, 32->16, 41->21, 65->37), so the item is decidable in seconds without ever forming the substitution u = sqrt(x-16). That is a cheaper path than the intended one, and it is not an option-set tell, it is a difficulty collapse.
SM17A-B2.note: Key verified. Labelled medium; with four integer options and every x-16 a perfect square, a plug-in solver finishes faster than the substitution solver, so easy. EDITORIAL DEFECT: the explanation carries an 'OPTION-SET NOTE, recorded because it is what this set was built for' aimed at a reviewer, not a student.

SM17A-B3.free_elimination: Simplified stem / perfect-square scan: because the exponent is 3/2, x-7 must be 125^(2/3) = (125^(1/3))^2, i.e. a perfect square. Across the options x-7 takes 5, 11, 18, 25 and exactly ONE of those is a perfect square, so all three distractors fall to a single structural observation. The author's own OPTION-SET NOTE checks two other channels (x-7 < 125, x-7 > 0) and misses this one entirely - the declared bounds are the inert ones. Caveat required by the run's rule: spotting 25 as the square is about as cheap as computing 5^2, so the strike is not dramatically cheaper than solving.
SM17A-B3.note: Key correct. Whole option set collapses to one perfect-square scan, and the item is a one-step exponent manipulation. Recommend dropping from an Advanced Math batch aimed at the module-2 hard route: not broken, just thin and free-decidable.

SM17A-B4.free_elimination: Interpolation bound: an exponential with b>1 is convex, so P(3) lies strictly BELOW the chord through (1,24) and (4,648). That chord's value at t=3 is 440 - which is printed as an option - so 440 and the larger 492 both fall with no arithmetic beyond recognising the linear-interpolation value. 72 then survives only against 216, and the qualitative reading 'three hours multiplies by 27, so two hours must multiply by much more than 3' finishes it. Sign: all positive. Echo: no printed value is an option (the author checked this and is right, but checked the wrong channel).
SM17A-B4.note: Key verified two ways (648/3 and 24*9). The two linear-model distractors are the standard SAT family, so I would not call this a leak, but the author's OPTION-SET NOTE rules out geometric-mean and printed-value tells while the live elimination - convexity against the chord - is undeclared. Same editorial defect: reviewer-facing note in the explanation.

SM17A-B5.free_elimination: none found. Sign: k must be positive since all zeros are positive, but all four options are positive. Parity/residue: 27, 29, 41, 44 share no usable class and k=41 is not distinguished. Closure: no option is the sum or product of others. Echo: 12 and 42 do not appear, and no option is 42 minus a printed number. Maclaurin's inequality (e2^2 >= 3*e1*e3 = 1512, so k >= 39) would strike 27 and 29, but that is not cheaper than simply factoring 42 - it is not a shortcut for this population.
SM17A-B5.note: Key correct: 2, 3, 7 is the unique positive-integer triple with product 42 and sum 12, and the explanation enumerates the alternatives correctly. Cleanest option set in the batch after A8.

SM17A-B6.free_elimination: Closure under the map the stem prints: one subtraction (3*3-8 = 1) reduces the question to 'which branch applies at x=1', and the option set contains BOTH branch values at 1 (-2 from 3x^2-5, 7 from 12-5x). So -3 and -41 fall together as values of f at inputs the transformation does not produce, and the item resolves to a 50/50 between the two boundary values for anyone who does not know that x<=1 belongs to the quadratic piece. Sign, parity, echo: nothing further.
SM17A-B6.note: Key correct; the boundary is closed on the quadratic side, so f(1) = -2. This is the intended discrimination and I would keep it, but the arithmetic is one substitution and the effective choice is binary, so easy rather than medium.

SM17A-B7.free_elimination: Printed-number echo: 2.5 is -b/(2a) = 20/8, computable straight from the two printed coefficients, and is the classic answered-the-wrong-question option - strikeable because it is a vertex ABSCISSA offered where an extreme VALUE is asked, and because it is the only option that is not plausibly a y-value of this parabola's scale. Sign: the discriminant 400-752 is negative so the minimum is positive and -3 falls, but that costs the same as completing the square, so it does not count as free. Monotonicity: min < f(0) = 47 holds for all four. Closure/parity: none.
SM17A-B7.note: Key correct: f(x) = 4(x-2.5)^2 + 22. Labelled medium, but a bare complete-the-square with no wrapper is an easy item on the module-2 hard route - the least demanding item in the batch.

SM17A-B8.free_elimination: Closure - the set contains the answer to the adjacent question: -7 is the PRODUCT of the two k values (the constant of k^2-18k-7) offered where the SUM is asked, so {18, -7} is a Vieta pair. That is a structural relation a solver can see the shape of but cannot use to choose a direction, so it strikes nothing on its own. Sign: the sum could be of either sign a priori. Parity/residue: 18 and 2 are even, 14 even, -7 odd - no class matches. Echo: 5 and 4 are printed but neither appears; 14 and 2 are not visibly derived from them.
SM17A-B8.note: Key correct: the discriminant condition gives k^2-18k-7=0 with sum 18, and the explanation is right that the two k values are irrational so they need not be found. The 'exactly one real solution for exactly two values of k' phrasing is slightly heavy but is accurate and prevents a solver from hunting a single nice k.
